note: Approved plain-language explanations for the chat. Every fact comes from MASTER_PLAN.md, docs/DATA_FACTS.md or contracts/API.md (see 'basis'). No safety or medical instructions here: those are fixed strings in get_prep. No ids, coordinates, line names or crew details.

passages.title: What the risk band means
passages.text: Your risk band (Low, Medium or High) compares your area with nearby homes in this region. It is not a percent chance that you will lose power. High means your area is among the homes most likely to be hit, based on where damage happened in past storms.

passages.title: Why we don't give a percent chance
passages.text: We show a band instead of a percent because our data comes from one region and two big storms. A percent would sound more exact than our data allows. The band is an honest comparison with nearby homes, not a promise either way.

passages.title: What the risk band is based on
passages.text: The band comes from a model that learned from past storm damage in this area. It looks at how often lines near you were damaged in earlier storms, whether your power comes through overhead lines, and how far down the line your home is.

passages.title: How homes are sorted into bands
passages.text: At the default storm strength, roughly the top 15 of every 100 homes in the area are High and the next 25 of every 100 are Medium. The rest are Low. When the storm strength changes, scores are compared with those same fixed cutoffs, so a stronger storm can move your band up.

passages.title: Why overhead lines matter
passages.text: If your power comes through overhead lines, ice and trees can hit them during a storm. That is one of the things that can raise your band. We know whether each home is served by overhead or underground lines from the utility's records.

passages.title: Why being far down the line matters
passages.text: Power reaches your home through a chain of equipment that starts at a substation. If your home is far down the line, behind several pieces of equipment, damage at any of them can cut your power. That can raise your band a little.

passages.title: What the confidence level means
passages.text: Confidence tells you how much history we have for your line. High means the line serving your home has at least 3 past damage records and we can trace the equipment that feeds your home. Low means fewer than 3 records, so we still show a band but with a limited history note.

passages.title: Why it says "We can't predict this reliably"
passages.text: Sometimes there are no past damage records on the line serving your home, or we could not trace which equipment feeds it. In that case we do not guess. We show no band and link you to the official outage page instead. It does not mean your home is safe or unsafe, only that we lack the history to say.

passages.title: Where to find the official outage information
passages.text: For official outage reports and updates, use the Appalachian Power outage page at https://www.appalachianpower.com/outages/.

passages.title: How we estimate when your power comes back
passages.text: We list the repairs reported on your line that are not fixed yet. We estimate how long each repair takes, decide which crews work on what, and run the whole thing 1,000 times with small random differences. The range you see, like "likely back in 6 to 14 hours", covers the middle 80 of every 100 simulated runs.
passages.basis: MASTER_PLAN Lane B 2, CLAUDE.md rule 6; contracts/mocks/restoration.json

passages.title: Why we give a range, not one time
passages.text: Repairs take different amounts of time, and new damage can be found. A single time would sound more certain than it is. A range is more honest: it is an estimate, not a promise, and the utility's confirmed time may differ.

passages.title: Where the repair hours come from
passages.text: Repair times come from AEP's labor workbook, which lists the hands-on hours to install and remove each kind of equipment, such as about 4.8 hours for a pole. We add extra time when a site is hard to reach or needs special equipment, then multiply by 4.5 for travel and setup, as the workbook does. Some wire hours are best guesses because the workbook has no wire unit.

passages.title: How we count repair crews
passages.text: We do not have real crew data. We assume one shared regional pool of 150 crews, split across lines by how much repair work each line has, with at least 1 crew per line. On each line, crews start with repairs closest to the substation, then the ones that bring back the most homes.

passages.title: Why your estimate changed
passages.text: Our estimate only knows about damage reported so far. When crews find new damage on your line, the range can jump later, and you get an "estimate updated" message. As repairs move forward, jobs already in progress only count their remaining time, so the range can also get shorter.

passages.title: Why the estimate and the outage feed can disagree
passages.text: Your estimate only uses damage that has been reported so far. When crews find more damage on your line, the estimate can move, and we send you an update.

passages.title: Why neighbors may get power back first
passages.text: Repairs happen in steps. Each home depends on the equipment between it and the substation, and a neighbor on a different branch may have fewer repairs in the way. So some neighbors may get power back before you, even on the same street.

passages.title: What the switching setting means
passages.text: Switching is a network assumption. When it is on (the default), we assume crews can reroute power around damage, so only the repairs on your home's own path matter. When it is off, you wait for every repair on your line, which usually makes the estimate longer.

passages.title: What the "What could change this?" card does
passages.text: This card lets you try what-ifs: more crews on your line, roads blocked by ice or trees, more damage found, or switching turned off. Each one re-runs our estimate. These change our estimate only, never the utility feed.

passages.title: What "roads blocked" does to the estimate
passages.text: When you turn on roads blocked by ice or trees, each repair gets between 2 and 8 extra hours in our estimate. That stands in for crews having trouble reaching the damage. The real records also note when a repair had an access issue.

passages.title: What the status steps mean
passages.text: The status tracker moves through four steps: damage reported and being assessed, crew assigned, repairing, and restored. these steps come from the utility feed, not real crew tracking. We never show crew names, locations or ids.

passages.title: How we know your power is out
passages.text: A damaged piece of equipment knocks out every home that gets power through it, from when it is reported until it is fixed. We trace each damage record to the equipment and homes it feeds, which works for about 99 of every 100 records.

passages.title: How we know your power is back
passages.text: The utility feed marks your home restored when the last repair on your home's path is finished. Then the app shows "Power's back" with a recap that compares our first range with what happened. A real system would confirm it with live data from the utility.

passages.title: Why we show our range next to what happened
passages.text: When power comes back, the recap puts our first estimate next to the actual restore time. We show it even when we were off. It helps you judge how much to trust the next estimate.

passages.title: What "Our estimate" means
passages.text: "Our estimate" marks a number our own models computed from real AEP data, like your risk band or restoration range. It is not from the utility and it is not a promise. Every number in the app carries a label so you know where it came from.

passages.title: What "Simulated utility feed" means
passages.text: "Utility feed" marks information about your line right now, such as whether your power is out and which repair step it is on.

passages.title: What "Utility confirmed" means
passages.text: "Utility confirmed" marks a restore time posted by the utility itself. Until the utility posts one, that spot stays empty and you see our estimate instead.

passages.title: What "Safety guidance" means
passages.text: "Safety guidance" marks safety and medical wording that was written and reviewed ahead of time. The assistant quotes it as written and never makes it up.

passages.title: Why there is no utility-confirmed time
passages.text: The utility may post its own estimated restore time during an outage. Until it does, the utility-confirmed time stays empty and we show our estimate as a range.

passages.title: Where our data comes from
passages.text: We use AEP's real records: 1,659 past damage records (from a system called ARCOS), a list of 117,642 homes with the line that serves each, a network map showing which equipment feeds each home, and AEP's labor workbook for repair hours. Homes are identified only by scrambled codes.

passages.title: What the damage records contain
passages.text: Each damage record says roughly where the damage was, what broke (for example a power line, a pole, fuse equipment or a transformer), whether there was an access issue, whether special equipment was needed, and the dates it was reported and repaired. The records have dates but no times of day.

passages.title: Does this work where I live?
passages.text: This app covers homes in Appalachian Power's area around Roanoke, Virginia. If you live elsewhere, it cannot tell you anything about your home. For any area, the official outage page is the right place to check.

passages.title: Why we don't use live weather
passages.text: We don't use live weather forecasts yet. Your risk band is based on where damage happened in past storms near you. Live weather would make the band better.

passages.title: Why there is no real crew information
passages.text: We don't show crew names, locations, or ids. The status tracker shows the step your repair is on: reported, crew assigned, repairing, or restored.

passages.title: Why repair records only have dates
passages.text: Past repair records show the day damage was reported and the day it was fixed, but not the hour. So we get repair hours from the labor workbook and use the dates to check our crew numbers. In the February 2025 storm, half the repairs were marked fixed within 1 day of the report and 9 in 10 within 2 days.

passages.title: Which records we leave out of repair-time numbers
passages.text: For repair-time numbers we leave out 76 records not marked as repaired and 138 records that were all closed on one date in October 2024, which looks like a bulk clean-up. Those records still count as past damage, just not for how long repairs take.

passages.title: What "past damage on your line" means
passages.text: Line history counts past damage records on the power line that serves your home, using only records from before the current time on the storm clock. "Lines like yours" groups a few other lines with a similar number of homes, equipment chain and damage history. They are added together and never named.

passages.title: What we never show
passages.text: We never show street addresses, house numbers or road names, exact locations (only areas about 1 km across), equipment or line ids, crew information, the locations of hospitals, fire stations or ambulances, or life-support flags from utility records. Your home is shown by a scrambled code, not your address.

passages.title: How your home is identified
passages.text: Each home is identified by a one-way scrambled code made from the utility's premise number with a secret salt. The code cannot be turned back into your address. Map areas are grouped into cells about 1 km across.

passages.title: What happens to the needs you tell us
passages.text: You can tell the app about a medical device, refrigerated medicine, mobility needs, well water, or a critical facility like a clinic, shelter or care home. These come only from your own choices, are sent with each request to tailor the guidance, and are never stored or logged. We never use the utility's life-support records about a person.

passages.title: What the app logs
passages.text: For checking the system, the app logs which screen or tool was used, the settings, the source label and the random seed. It does not log your chat messages or any needs you declared.

passages.title: How the assistant answers
passages.text: The assistant only talks. Every number it gives comes from our code, such as the risk band or the restoration range. Safety and medical wording is fixed text written in advance. If the AI is not available, you get answers built from the same numbers.

passages.title: Why you get the same numbers each time
passages.text: Our simulations use fixed random seeds, so the same inputs always give the same results. If a number changes, it is because something changed, like new damage being reported or a what-if setting.

passages.title: When the app sends alerts
passages.text: The app sends a pre-storm alert when your band is Medium or High, a message when your outage is confirmed, an "estimate updated" message when the expected time moves by more than 3 hours or more than a quarter, and a message when power is back.

passages.title: How alerts reach you
passages.text: Alerts come as push notifications by default, and as text messages when your phone is in low-power mode. If you declared a medical need or a critical facility and the outage may last more than 12 hours, the app offers a call.

passages.title: What low-power mode does
passages.text: Low-power mode saves your battery: dark screen, text only, no map and no animation. It still shows your status, the restoration range, the confidence, one next step and the safety line.

passages.title: What would make this better
passages.text: Live weather feeds would sharpen the risk band. Smart-meter pings would show right away when a home loses or gets back power. A true history of restore times, with hours and not just dates, and crew data would make the restoration range tighter.
